content: A speculum is a medical instrument designed to facilitate the examination of body cavities. Its structure varies depending on the specific cavity it is intended to investigate. Historically, the speculum has also been referred to as a diopter or dioptra in older medical texts. Vaginal specula were utilized as far back as Roman times, with artifacts discovered in Pompeii providing evidence of their use. The vaginal speculum, as developed by J. Marion Sims, consists of a hollow cylindrical structure with a rounded end. This cylinder is divided into two hinged parts, resembling the beak of a duck. The device is inserted into the vagina to dilate it, allowing for visual examination of the vaginal walls and the cervix. A specialized variant of the vaginal speculum, known as the weighted speculum, features a broad half-tube bent at approximately a 90-degree angle. The external side of the angle contains the channel of the tube, and one end is equipped with a spherical metal weight. This weighted speculum is used during vaginal surgeries, particularly when the patient is positioned in the lithotomy position. The weight stabilizes the speculum, freeing the surgeon’s hands for other tasks. Vaginal specula are also employed in anal surgeries, although there are other types of anal specula available. One common design is the sigmoidoscope, which resembles a tube with a removable, bullet-shaped insert. When inserted into the rectum, the insert dilates the rectum to match the diameter of the tube. Once the insert is removed, the tube remains in place, enabling examination of the rectum. This design is one of the oldest surgical instruments still in use, with historical examples dating back several centuries. Ear specula are shaped like funnels and are available in various sizes to accommodate different needs. Nasal specula, on the other hand, consist of two flat blades connected to a handle. The instrument is hinged, so when the handles are squeezed together, the blades spread apart laterally, allowing for examination of the nasal cavity. Traditionally, all specula were constructed from metal and sterilized after each use. However, many modern specula, particularly those used in emergency departments and outpatient clinics, are now made of plastic. These plastic versions are sterile, disposable, and intended for single use. In contrast, specula used in surgical settings are still commonly made of metal. In some cases, vaginal and anal specula have been repurposed as sex toys. Despite misconceptions, the use of a speculum does not cause damage to the vaginal opening, as confirmed by many gynecological experts. In a few U.S. states, the personal use of vaginal specula is restricted by law. However, due to the influence of the second-wave feminist movement, which promoted cervical self-examination, many states have relaxed or entirely removed these restrictions. Nonetheless, distributors of specula must adhere to specific guidelines regarding which types of specula can be sold.
